title: Bone and joint X-ray
what: A picture of your bones and joints taken with X-rays. It shows fractures, cracks, and changes in the joints.
why: After an injury, for joint or back pain, or to check how a fracture is healing.
tell_doctor: If you are pregnant or could be pregnant
If it hurts to move. Staff will help you lie down or stand up
If you have metal in a bone after surgery

prepare.title: Preparation
prepare.text: None needed for arms, legs, and joints. You can eat and drink.

prepare.title: Lower back and tailbone
prepare.text: Sometimes you are asked to eat fewer gas-causing foods the day before and to empty your bowels. Check with your clinic.

prepare.title: Metal
prepare.text: Take off jewelry, watches, and anything metal from the part of the body being X-rayed.

bring: Past X-rays of the same body part, to compare
steps: You uncover the body part being checked
The radiographer places it on the table or plate in the right position
The rest of your body may be covered with a protective apron
You need to keep still for a couple of seconds while the picture is taken
Usually 2 pictures are taken in different positions
feel: You do not feel the X-ray itself
After an injury, holding the position can hurt. Tell the radiographer
after: You can go back to your day straight away
The images and report are usually ready the same day
Take the results to the doctor who referred you
red_flags: After an injury, the arm or leg turns blue, goes numb, swells a lot, or the bone looks out of shape: call emergency services

faq.q: Can an X-ray show ligaments and the meniscus?
faq.a: No. An X-ray shows bones. Ligaments, menisci, and cartilage are seen better on MRI or ultrasound.
A fracture can hide on one picture. Two positions give an accurate view.
